title: Web Applications and Services
text:
Preface
This textbook is a self-study resource for the theoretical component of Web Applications and Services (ASW), Master’s in Electrical and Computer Engineering (MEEC), covering Web application architecture, best development practices, the HTTP protocol, HTML and CSS, server-side and client-side programming, database access, and REST Web Services, with Java EE as the case study.

title: Web Applications and Services
text:
Organisation
The textbook is organised into three thematic blocks:

Web Foundations — client-server architecture, HTML, CSS and the HTTP protocol
Classic Java EE — Servlets, the stateful model and session management
Web Services — security and filters, and REST Web Services, including consuming an API from JavaScript in the browser

The practical LABs (the same as ESIGELEC’s, with a JavaScript front-office added in LAB6) are described in Appendices D1 to D6, with the development environment setup in Appendix C.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.1 The Problem: Building a Web Application from Scratch
A Web application is not simply a program that runs on a single computer: it is a program that answers requests coming from multiple clients, simultaneously, over the network. Built from scratch, with no supporting platform, an application of this kind would have to solve, on its own, a set of problems common to any system of this sort:
Solving all of these problems again and again, application after application, would be a waste of effort. This is exactly why enterprise platforms exist, providing these services ready to use, and freeing developers to focus on the business logic of the application.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.2 Two Orientations: Presentation vs. Service
A Web application can follow two distinct orientations, depending on the kind of response it produces:

Presentation-oriented

Generates interactive Web pages (HTML, CSS and dynamic content) in response to each request. This is the traditional Web application model, meant to be consumed directly by a human user through a browser.

Service-oriented

Implements the endpoint of a Web service, typically returning structured data in JSON or XML format instead of HTML. This model is meant to be consumed by another program: a mobile application, a single-page application, or another service.


This distinction largely maps onto the split between front-end (the part of the application that interacts directly with whoever uses it) and back-end (the part that processes logic and data). A presentation-oriented application tends to blend these two responsibilities into a single server-side component; a service-oriented application separates them clearly, leaving the front-end entirely up to the client.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.3 The MVC Pattern
Organising all of an application’s code as a single undifferentiated block quickly becomes unmanageable: the code that processes the request, the code that accesses data, and the code that generates the response end up tangled together, hard to test or change independently. The Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern solves this by splitting the application into three distinct responsibilities:

Model

Represents the application’s data and business logic, independently of how it is presented. In a Web application, the Model is typically responsible for accessing the database and returning already-validated information.

View

Responsible for presenting the data to whoever requests it, without containing business logic. In a presentation-oriented application, the View generates HTML; in a service-oriented application, there is, in fact, no server-side View at all: the response is just structured data (JSON), and it is the client that decides how to present it.

Controller

Receives the request, decides which operation to perform on the Model, and chooses the View (or response format) to return. The Controller is what bridges the incoming HTTP request and the application’s logic.


This separation of responsibilities is one of the most recurring design principles throughout this subject. It shows up in its classic form when a server-side component acts as Controller and delegates presentation to another, which acts as View; and it shows up in a far less obvious form when the View stops existing on the server side and is instead rebuilt in the browser, from JSON data.

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
section: 1.4 Three Pieces: Frontend, Middleware and Backend
text:
1.4 Three Pieces: Frontend, Middleware and Backend
Both the presentation/service distinction and the MVC pattern describe the same central idea, seen from different angles: a Web application is not a single block, but a set of pieces with distinct roles, communicating with one another. Throughout this course, those pieces always reduce to the same three:

Frontend

The part of the application that runs on the client side (typically a browser), responsible for presenting information and collecting input from whoever uses it. It largely corresponds to the View in MVC.

Middleware

The protocol that connects the Frontend to the Backend, carrying requests and responses between the two. In this course, that protocol is always HTTP.

Backend

The part of the application that runs on the server side, responsible for business logic and data access. It largely corresponds to the Model and the Controller in MVC.


This three-way division is the map for the rest of this book: first the Frontend is built (Chapter 2, in HTML/CSS/Bootstrap), then the Middleware that connects it to the server is studied in detail (Chapter 3, the HTTP protocol), and only then is the Backend built that actually answers those requests (from Chapter 4 onward, with Servlets and, later, REST APIs).

title: 1  Web Application Architecture
text:
1.5 The Client-Server Model
The Middleware connecting the Frontend to the Backend rests on the client-server model: the Frontend (typically a browser) sends a request over the network, and the Backend processes that request and returns a response.






Figure 1.1: The client (for example, a browser) sends an HTTP request; the server processes it and returns a response. The exchange repeats at every interaction, without the server, by itself, retaining memory of the previous one.



This exchange takes place through the HTTP protocol (HyperText Transfer Protocol), which has two fundamental characteristics:

It is transaction-oriented: each interaction consists of a request followed by a response
It is stateless: the server does not, by itself, retain any memory of a client’s previous requests

The absence of state at the protocol level does not prevent an application from needing to retain information across requests (for instance, to know that a user is authenticated). That need is addressed at the application level, not the protocol level, through mechanisms such as sessions and cookies (see Chapter 5).
The details of this protocol, the Middleware connecting these two pieces, are the subject of Chapter 3.

title: 3  The HTTP Protocol
text:
3.1 The Middleware Connecting Frontend and Backend
Chapter 1 identified three components in any Web application: Frontend, Middleware and Backend. Chapter 2 was devoted to the first of these, a set of HTML pages with forms, including the capital-lookup form (capital.html) and the authentication form (login.html). On their own, these forms do nothing: they need a protocol to carry the data the user fills in to a server, and to bring a response back. That protocol, the Middleware used in Web applications, is HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol). This chapter details how it works.

title: 3  The HTTP Protocol
text:
3.2 The TCP/IP Model
Before going into the details of HTTP itself, it is worth recalling where this protocol fits into the communications stack. The TCP/IP model organises that stack into four layers, each responsible for a different aspect of network communication:








Layer
Responsibility
Example protocols




Application
The format of the data exchanged between applications
HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS


Transport
Delivery of data between processes, reliable (TCP) or not (UDP)
TCP, UDP


Internet
Routing of data between networks, by IP address
IP


Network Access
Physical transmission of data on the local medium
Ethernet, Wi-Fi









Figure 3.1: The four-layer TCP/IP model. HTTP lives at the Application layer, and rests on TCP (Transport layer) to guarantee that data arrives reliably and in the correct order.



HTTP is, therefore, an Application-layer protocol: it is not concerned with how the data reaches its destination, only with defining the format of the request and the response. That delivery is TCP’s responsibility, at the Transport layer, which guarantees that the data arrives complete, error-free, and in the order it was sent — a guarantee that HTTP depends on, without ever implementing it directly.

title: 3  The HTTP Protocol
text:
3.3 HTTP
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a text-based protocol, based on the request-response model: the client sends a request, the server returns a response, and the connection between the two retains no memory of previous requests — each request is handled independently, that is, HTTP has no state (it is stateless). This section details the three aspects that define a request and a response: methods, the general message format, and status codes.

3.3.1 Methods
Every request from the client to the server is made in HTTP format and indicates, through a method, the operation intended for a given resource. The “resource” in the context of Web applications can be an html page, an image, a PDF, or any other item capable of being manipulated digitally:



Method
Typical semantics




GET
Retrieve a resource


POST
Create a resource


PUT
Update or replace a resource


DELETE
Remove a resource


HEAD
Retrieve headers only, no body



These five methods cover the vast majority of operations performed by a Web application; the first two (GET and POST) are by far the most common in Web pages, while PUT and DELETE become more important mainly in Web services.


3.3.2 Message Format
When the application on the client’s computer wants to communicate with the server, it activates the Application layer of the communications protocol stack, which formats the request according to the HTTP protocol. Both a request and the response that follows it share a similar general message structure:

A first line, differing between a request (method, URL and HTTP version) and a response (HTTP version, status code and reason)
A set of headers, carrying metadata about the message (for instance, the destination host, the content type, or its length)
An optional body, holding the actual data

A GET request typically has no body: all the data it carries goes in the URL itself, as parameters. A POST request carries its data in the message body, outside the URL.






Figure 3.2: The general format of an HTTP message: the first line (different for a request and a response), followed by the various groups of headers, and finally the body.




Example: From the Capital-Lookup Form to an HTTP Request
Recall the capital-lookup form built in Chapter 2 (capital.html):
<form method="GET" action="/capital">
  <label for="countrycode">Código do país</label>
  <input type="text" id="countrycode" name="countrycode">
  <button type="submit">Consultar</button>
</form>
This HTML code renders in the browser as shown in figure Figure 3.3:






Figure 3.3: The capital-lookup form (capital.html), as displayed in the browser.



When submitted (by clicking the Consultar button) with the value PT in the input, the browser generates the following GET HTTP request:

GET /capital?countrycode=PT HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080

Note that, because this is a GET method, the countrycode parameter is sent as part of the URL (after the ?), and there is no body in the message. If the same form used method="POST", the parameter would instead travel in the request body, and the URL would stay clean (/capital).
The server, upon processing this request, returns an HTTP response such as the following:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
{"country": "Portugal", "capital": "Lisboa", "ccode": "PT"}



Example: From the Authentication Form to a POST Request with a Body
Now recall the authentication form, also from Chapter 2 (login.html), with the fields user and pass:
<form method="POST" action="/login">
  <label for="user">Utilizador</label>
  <input type="text" id="user" name="user">
  <label for="pass">Palavra-passe</label>
  <input type="password" id="pass" name="pass">
  <button type="submit">Entrar</button>
</form>
This HTML code renders in the browser as shown in figure Figure 3.4:






Figure 3.4: The authentication form (login.html), as displayed in the browser.



When submitted, this form generates the following HTTP request:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 21
user=javaee&pass=asw2026

Unlike the previous example, the parameters no longer go in the URL: they follow in the request body, after a blank line separating the headers from the body. This is why credentials and other sensitive data are typically sent via POST, never GET: a request body is not recorded in browser history or in the server’s log files, unlike URL parameters.
Upon successfully validating the credentials, the server returns an HTTP response such as the following — in this case, a presentation-oriented application (see Chapter 1), which returns HTML code in the response body, ready to render in the browser. If the application were service-oriented, the response body would instead carry JSON rather than HTML:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
<h1>Bem-vindo, javaee</h1>
<p>Sessão iniciada com sucesso.</p>




3.3.3 Status Codes
Every HTTP response includes a numeric status code, briefly indicating the outcome of the request. Codes are grouped into five categories, based on the leading digit:



Range
Category




1xx
Informational


2xx
Success


3xx
Redirection


4xx
Client error


5xx
Server error



Within these categories, a handful of codes come up particularly often when developing Web services:







Code
Meaning




200 OK
The request was processed successfully


201 Created
A new resource was successfully created


400 Bad Request
The request is malformed, or a required parameter is missing


403 Forbidden
The client lacks permission to access the resource


404 Not Found
The requested resource does not exist


500 Internal Server Error
An unhandled error occurred on the server side



Choosing the right status code for each situation is an essential part of designing a Web service: the code, by itself, conveys information the client can use to decide how to react, without needing to parse the response body.

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.1 The Jakarta EE Platform
With the Frontend built (Chapter 2) and the Middleware detailed (Chapter 3), what remains is the third piece identified in Chapter 1: the Backend, which actually receives HTTP requests and answers them. That is the subject of this chapter and the ones that follow.
Jakarta EE (previously known as Java EE, until it was renamed in 2019) is a platform that provides a ready-to-use set of services and APIs to deal with the problems common to any Web application (see Chapter 1), freeing developers to focus on the application’s business logic.
The platform rests on the Java language and the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which means any component written for Jakarta EE benefits from the portability and automatic memory management already familiar from the language.

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.2 Layered Architecture
The Jakarta EE platform organises an application according to a model distributed across several layers (tiers), each with a well-defined role and typically installed on a different machine:








Tier
Where it resides
Typical components




Client Tier
Client machine
Web pages (browser), client applications


Web Tier
Jakarta EE server
Servlets, JavaServer Pages, Web Services


Business Tier
Jakarta EE server
Enterprise Beans (business logic)


EIS Tier (Enterprise Information System)
Database server
Databases, enterprise information systems



This layering allows each component to evolve relatively independently of the others: changing the database does not require rewriting the business logic, and changing the client interface does not require changing the server.






Figure 4.1: The layered architecture of Jakarta EE: the client communicates only with the Web Tier, which in turn relies on the Business Tier and, through it, on the database in the EIS Tier.









Tomcat is not a complete Jakarta EE server



Apache Tomcat, used throughout this course, is a Servlet Container: it implements only the Web Tier (Servlets, JSP). It does not include support for Enterprise Beans nor for the Business Tier itself, unlike a complete Jakarta EE application server (for example, WildFly, WebSphere or GlassFish). In practice, this means that the business logic which, in the formal architecture, would belong to the Business Tier, is implemented here directly in plain Java classes, rather than in Enterprise Beans.
crumbs: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
text:
4.3 Why Servlets?
Implementing, from scratch, a Java program capable of answering HTTP requests would require solving, on its own, a set of problems common to any Web server: parsing the incoming HTTP message, managing several connections at once (each in its own thread), controlling the life cycle of the in-memory instances, and packaging all of this into a format that an application server knows how to install and start.
A Servlet is a Java class that runs inside a Servlet Container (for example, Apache Tomcat) and automatically receives all of this work already done:

Parsing of the HTTP request
Thread management, one per request
Management of the Servlet’s own life cycle
Its own deployment model, packaged in a .war file (Web Application Archive)

The Servlet Container corresponds, in the layered architecture presented above, to the Web Tier: it is there that Servlets reside, between the client and the business layer.






Figure 4.2: From the client’s point of view, a Servlet is just another destination for HTTP requests: it receives a request, returns a response.
crumbs: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
section: 4.4 The Life Cycle of a Servlet
text:
4.4 The Life Cycle of a Servlet
When a request is routed to a Servlet, the container always follows the same sequence (see Figure 4.3):

If no instance of that Servlet yet exists in memory, the container loads the class, creates an instance, and calls the init() method
For each request received, the container invokes the service() method, which dispatches to doGet(), doPost(), or another method depending on the HTTP verb used, passing it the request and response objects
If the container needs to remove the Servlet (for example, when shutting down the server), it invokes the destroy() method

An important detail follows from this: there is a single instance of each Servlet in memory, even if N clients are using the same service at once. Each request is handled by a different thread, but all of those threads share the same instance. In practice, this means:






Beware of shared state



Never store data specific to one request in the Servlet’s instance attributes: since the instance is shared by all threads, one request can read or overwrite data belonging to another request in progress. Local variables, declared inside doGet() or doPost(), are safe, because each thread has its own copy.








Figure 4.3: The container loads the Servlet’s class only once; each incoming request is dispatched to its own thread, which invokes service() on that same shared instance.
crumbs: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals

title: 4  Java EE and Servlet Fundamentals
section: 4.5 From the HTTP Message to the Java Method
text:
4.5 From the HTTP Message to the Java Method
A Servlet is bound to a URL through the @WebServlet annotation, which maps a path to the class that will handle it:
@WebServlet("/country")
public class CountryServlet extends HttpServlet {
    // ...
}
A client request to http://localhost:8080/country is thus routed to the CountryServlet class. The container automatically builds, from the elements of the incoming HTTP message (see Chapter 3 (cap03.qmd)), the request object; the complementary response object is what the Servlet uses to build the outgoing message. The elements of each message correspond to concrete methods of these two objects:



HTTP element
Java access
When it is used




Request headers
request.getHeader(name)
Always, regardless of the type of request


Parameters (GET query string, or application/x-www-form-urlencoded body of a POST)
request.getParameter(name)
Traditional HTML forms (see Chapter 2), in a presentation-oriented application


Raw request body (typically JSON)
request.getInputStream()
REST Web services (see Chapter 7): the body does not arrive in application/x-www-form-urlencoded format, so getParameter() does not parse it, and the JSON must be read and parsed manually


Writing the response
response.getWriter() or response.getOutputStream()
Always, regardless of the type of response



protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) {
    String countryCode = request.getParameter("countrycode");
    // ...
}






Figure 4.4: Inside the Jakarta EE server, the request arrives wrapped in an HttpServletRequest, is processed by the Web component (the Servlet), which may call another servlet, or query data resources, and the response goes out wrapped in an HttpServletResponse.

4.8 Servlets and the MVC Pattern: the Missing View
This course focuses mainly on Web service applications, so the Servlets presented always return JSON: being service-oriented, they in fact have no View at all (see Chapter 1). This does not mean the application cannot feed a graphical view; in that case the MVC model is used, with the Servlet acting as Controller and feeding a Web page indirectly through JSON. That Web page is naturally built in HTML, but needs some script logic that extracts the necessary data from the JSON and places it in the right spots on the HTML page (see Chapter 8).
If the application is, from the ground up, presentation-oriented, however, the same Servlet that acts as Controller can generate the page’s HTML (the View) directly, or it can delegate that responsibility to a dedicated page, using a technology known as JSP (JavaServer Pages), keeping MVC’s separation of responsibilities, as shown in Figure 4.5.






Figure 4.5: In the classic realisation of MVC in Jakarta EE, the Servlet acts as Controller, a JavaServer Page as View, and a plain Java class as Model.



That dedicated page, the JavaServer Page (JSP), is covered in detail in Chapter 5.

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
text:
5.1 HTTP Is Stateless: the Problem
The HTTP protocol is stateless (see Chapter 1): each request is independent, and the server does not, by itself, retain any memory of previous requests. At the protocol level, there is no notion whatsoever of a “user with an active session”.
This raises an immediate practical problem: if a user authenticates in one request, how does a following request, minutes later, know that this user is still authenticated? The answer relies on two complementary mechanisms:

HttpSession: an object stored on the server side, associated with an identifier that the client returns on every request

title: 5  The Stateful Model: Sessions and JSP
text:
5.3 Sessions (HttpSession)
Storing state on the server side requires a dedicated object: the HttpSession. A session is obtained, or created, from the request:
HttpSession session = request.getSession();          // creates it if it doesn't exist
HttpSession session = request.getSession(true);      // equivalent, explicit
HttpSession session = request.getSession(false);     // NEVER creates one; returns null if there isn't one
Once obtained, the session stores and returns information through attributes, and can be explicitly terminated:
session.setAttribute("email", "foo@fool.com");
String email = (String) session.getAttribute("email");
session.invalidate();                    // ends the session
session.setMaxInactiveInterval(1800);     // inactivity time, in seconds
One piece is still missing: if HTTP has no memory of previous requests, how does the server know that two successive requests belong to the same session? The answer is, once again, cookies: by convention, the session identifier travels in a cookie named JSESSIONID, automatically created by the Servlet Container on the first call to getSession().

JSESSIONID=22562577CE80EF3B1DAAA0E48F2B6392

When the client does not accept cookies, there is an alternative: encoding the session identifier directly in the URL.

http://localhost:8080/CapitaisAPI/country;jsessionid=829F8836C240B51DD2F074259F242833

It is good practice to always call response.encodeURL(url) when building a destination URL: if cookies are active, the method returns the URL unchanged; if they are not, it automatically appends the jsessionid.

section: 5.5 The MVC Pattern with Servlet and JSP
text:
5.5 The MVC Pattern with Servlet and JSP
Chapter 1 introduced the MVC pattern at a conceptual level, and Chapter 4 showed how a Servlet acts as Controller. The pages built in Chapter 2 already play the role of View, but they are static: their content does not change depending on the request. This section shows an alternative way of building the View — this time generated dynamically on the server side, from the data the Controller hands it.






Figure 5.1: The general MVC model, applicable to any interface (not just Web): the Controller updates the Model and the presentation; the View reads the Model to render itself.



In a presentation-oriented application, the Servlet receives the request and decides what to show, but delegates the actual generation of HTML to a JavaServer Page (JSP). The Model, in turn, is a plain Java class (for example, a DAO), independent of both.
The Servlet connects to the JSP through a RequestDispatcher: it places the data to be shown in a request attribute, and forwards the request itself to the page:
request.setAttribute("user", user);
request.getRequestDispatcher("/home.jsp").forward(request, response);
A JSP is a text document that mixes two kinds of content: static HTML and dynamic script elements. The first time it is requested, the Servlet Container automatically converts it into a Servlet class, which from then on behaves exactly like any other Servlet, in the role of Controller.

5.7 Lifecycle and Implicit Objects
A JSP’s lifecycle follows the same model as the Servlet it is converted into (see Chapter 4), with two details of its own:

The container automatically recompiles the JSP whenever the .jsp file changes
Instead of init() and destroy(), the JSP offers the methods jspInit() and jspDestroy()

Another practical difference: inside a JSP, a set of objects is automatically available, with no prior declaration, called implicit objects:



Implicit object
Type




out
JspWriter


request
HttpServletRequest


response
HttpServletResponse


session
HttpSession


page
Object



Because of the implicit object out, a JSP never needs to explicitly obtain a PrintWriter: out is used directly.

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
6.1 The Problem: Security Repeated in Every Servlet
With what has been presented so far (see Chapter 5), authentication is solved: the LoginServlet validates the credentials and stores the user in the session, and each protected endpoint checks that session at the start of its doGet() or doPost(). This works, but it has a hidden cost: the authentication logic lives, duplicated, inside every protected Servlet.
This duplication brings several problems along with it:
Put another way, this duplication violates the DRY principle (Don’t Repeat Yourself): a responsibility should live in a single place, and repeated logic increases the maintenance cost whenever that logic needs to change. More concretely, this design violates the Single Responsibility Principle: each Servlet ends up with two distinct responsibilities, its own business logic, and the security logic imposed on it. This makes security policies hard to evolve, and the design poorly scalable, both in number of endpoints and in the complexity of the access rules.

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
The same session check is repeated in every protected endpoint
There is a real risk of inconsistency between these copies
It is easy to forget the protection when creating a new endpoint

title: 6  Security and Filters
6  Security and Filters
text:
6.3 What a Filter Is
The question left unanswered is where the security logic should live: inside each Servlet? Duplicated across every endpoint? Or centralised in a single component? Security is, by nature, a cross-cutting concern: it runs through the whole application, rather than belonging to a single module. This is exactly what the Filter exists for.
A Filter is a server-side component that intercepts HTTP requests:

It runs before the destination Servlet
It can also run after the Servlet (over the response)
It can block, redirect, or modify the request or the response

Beyond authentication and authorisation, Filters are the natural mechanism for other cross-cutting concerns: activity logging, CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), or input validation. A Filter separates these concerns from the business logic, which stays exclusively in the Servlet.

title: 6  Security and Filters
section: 6.4 Where a Filter Sits in the Request
text:
6.4 Where a Filter Sits in the Request
One or more Filters can be chained between the client and the Servlet that actually handles the request:
Client → Filter 1 → ... → Filter N → Servlet (business logic) → Response






Figure 6.1: A request passes through the Filter chain before reaching the Servlet; each Filter can block the request (red), modify it (yellow), or let it proceed (green, by calling chain.doFilter()).



Each Filter in the chain has, essentially, three possible behaviours:

Block the request: for example, 400 (invalid data), 401 (invalid identity) or 403 (authenticated but without permission)
Modify the request: data normalisation and validation, activity logging, among others
Let it proceed: by calling chain.doFilter(request, response), passing control to the next element in the chain

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
6.5 A Filter’s Lifecycle
A Filter’s lifecycle follows the same model already presented for Servlets (see Chapter 4):

init(): executed once, when the container puts the Filter into service
doFilter(): executed on every request; it can inspect, block or modify the request and the response, and must call chain.doFilter() to continue the chain
destroy(): executed once, when the Filter is taken out of service, to free resources

Just like a Servlet, there is a single instance of each Filter, shared by multiple concurrent requests: exactly the same care already mentioned in Chapter 4 applies here — avoid shared mutable state, and prefer local variables inside doFilter().






Figure 6.2: A Filter’s lifecycle mirrors a Servlet’s: init() and destroy() run once, doFilter() runs on every request, for multiple concurrent requests.

title: 6  Security and Filters
section: 6.6 Servlet and Filter: Separation of Responsibilities
text:
6.6 Servlet and Filter: Separation of Responsibilities
Centralising security in a Filter reorganises the responsibilities of the whole application:






Figure 6.3: Without a Filter, each Servlet accumulates authentication, logging, validation and business logic. With a Filter, those cross-cutting concerns are concentrated in a single place, and each Servlet is left with only its own business logic.



This reorganisation brings concrete advantages:

The authentication logic is written once (DRY principle)
The security policy is applied consistently to every endpoint
There is no longer any risk of “forgetting” the protection on a new Servlet
The separation between cross-cutting concerns (Filter) and business logic (Servlet) becomes clear

title: 6  Security and Filters
6  Security and Filters
text:
6.8 Redirection vs. 401: an Architectural Difference
The correct way to react to an authentication failure depends on the kind of application:

In a traditional, presentation-oriented Web application (see Chapter 1), the natural response is a redirect to the login page (code 302)
In a REST API, whose contract is JSON (see Chapters 7 and 8), the correct response is to return 401, with no redirection at all

The difference boils down to one sentence: in a traditional Web application, an authentication failure changes the page shown; in a REST API, it only changes the status code returned. It is the client, not the server, that decides what to do next with that 401.

title: 6  Security and Filters
text:
6.9 Preparing for Stateless Security
The model presented in this chapter rests entirely on sessions: the server stores the authenticated user’s state (HttpSession), and the Filter checks that session on every request. This model has one limitation: it requires the server to keep memory of each user, which becomes problematic as soon as there is more than one server instance (see Chapter 8).
The alternative is token-based authentication: instead of the server storing any session at all, each request itself carries, on every call, all the information needed to authenticate. This shift, from a stateful model to a stateless model, is the subject of the following chapters.

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.1 The Problem: Applications That Need to Communicate
Up to this point, the server has always been thought of from the perspective of a single kind of client: a browser, requesting HTML pages for a human user to read. But a server rarely serves only that kind of client. A mobile application, another server, an integration script, or the JavaScript running in the browser itself (see Chapter 8) may also need to access the same information — without any of them needing, or wanting, to receive a ready-to-display HTML page.
HTML is a format designed for presentation: it mixes data with the form, or semantic structure, in which that data should be shown. A program that only needs the data (for example, the price of a product, or a country’s capital) would have to “take apart” the HTML to get to it — fragile, and dependent on presentation details that have nothing to do with the information itself. What is needed is a way of exposing the same data so that any program, not just a browser with a human looking at it, can consume it directly.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.2 What a Web Service Is
A Web Service is a software component accessible over the network — typically via HTTP — that exposes functionality or data in a format designed to be consumed by other programs, not read directly by a human. Unlike a Web page, a Web Service does not generate presentation: it returns structured data with no semantic dressing, and it is the client that decides what to do with it.
This decoupling is what allows the same server to answer, with the same logic, requests coming from completely different sources: a mobile application, a JavaScript front-office, or another server — all receive the same data, in the same structure, and each decides how to present it (or whether to present it at all).
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.3 SOAP and REST: Two Approaches
Historically, there have been two main approaches to building Web Services:

SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)

A formal, XML-based protocol, with a rigid message structure (the SOAP envelope) and a contract described separately, in a WSDL document. It is verbose and requires specific tooling to generate and consume that contract, but it offers strong formal guarantees — used mostly in legacy enterprise systems, with strict transaction and security requirements.

REST (Representational State Transfer)

An architectural style, not a formal protocol, that uses HTTP directly as both transport and contract: the verbs, status codes and headers already seen in Chapters 3 and 4 are, themselves, the vocabulary of the API. It is lighter, simpler to test, and is the dominant approach today for Web and mobile applications — the only one covered in detail in this course.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.4 REST: Fielding’s Principles
The term REST was coined by Roy Fielding, in 2000, to describe the architectural style that was already, in practice, implicit in the design of the Web itself. A REST service follows a set of principles:

Client-server: responsibilities are separated; the client does not need to know how the data is stored, and the server does not need to know how it is presented,
Stateless: each request contains all the information needed to be processed, without depending on memory of previous requests on the server (see Section 7.9),
Uniform interface: resources are always manipulated the same way, through HTTP’s own verbs and status codes, without inventing a bespoke vocabulary per API,
Resources and representations: everything the API exposes is modelled as a resource, identified by a URL, with one or more possible representations (typically JSON),
Cacheable: a response can indicate whether or not it may be cached, to avoid unnecessary repeated requests.

Not every API that calls itself “REST” strictly follows all of these principles — in practice, “REST” has become a generic term for “resource-oriented API over HTTP, typically with JSON”. That is the sense used throughout this course.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.5 Resource-Oriented Architecture
REST’s most visible principle is thinking of the API around resources, not actions. A resource is anything that can be identified and manipulated — a country, a user, an order — and it is identified by a URL, never by a function name.
A design that does not follow this principle is closer to an RPC (Remote Procedure Call) style, where the URL names an operation:

GET /getCountry?code=PT
GET /deleteCountry?code=PT

A resource-oriented design uses the URL itself to identify the resource, leaving the HTTP verb (see Chapter 3) to indicate the operation to perform on it:

GET /country/PT → get country PT
DELETE /country/PT → remove country PT

The advantage is not just aesthetic: it makes the API predictable. Once the /country/{code} pattern is known, it is immediately clear how to access, update or remove any country, without needing to memorise a different function name for each operation.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.6 HTTP Methods as the API’s Contract
text:
7.6 HTTP Methods as the API’s Contract
In a REST API, HTTP methods stop being just “the way the request arrives” (see Chapter 3) and become the API’s own contract: the meaning of each verb, applied to a resource, is always the same.



Method
Operation
Idempotent?




GET
Read the resource
Yes


POST
Create a new resource
No


PUT
Update or replace the resource
Yes


DELETE
Remove the resource
Yes



A method is said to be idempotent when repeating it several times has exactly the same effect as executing it once. DELETE /country/PT removes country PT; repeating the same request does not remove “anything more”, the final result is identical. POST /country, on the other hand, creates a new resource on every call, so it is not idempotent: repeating the request creates several resources, not just one. This property matters especially on unreliable networks: a client unsure whether a PUT or DELETE request reached its destination can safely repeat it; the same cannot be done with a POST, on pain of duplicating the created resource.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.7 JSON as a Resource’s Representation
A resource can have more than one possible representation — the same country could, in theory, be returned in JSON, in XML, or in any other format, depending on what the client requests. In practice, and throughout this course, the representation used is always JSON (the format traditionally associated with SOAP is XML, more verbose and less straightforward to generate and parse in JavaScript).
{"code": "PT", "name": "Portugal", "capital": "Lisboa"}
The Content-Type: application/json header (see Chapter 4) is what informs the client that this is the representation chosen for the response.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.8 From a Web Application to a REST Service
text:
7.8 From a Web Application to a REST Service
The infrastructure behind a REST service is nothing new: it is still a Servlet, mapped to a URL through @WebServlet (see Chapter 4), receiving an HTTP request and returning a response. What changes is what that response contains, and who it is designed for.
In a presentation-oriented application (see Chapters 1 and 5), the Servlet returns HTML, meant for a human to read directly in the browser. In a REST API, the same Servlet returns JSON, meant to be interpreted by code — whether that code is another server, a mobile application, or the browser’s own JavaScript (see Chapter 8). The View, in the classic MVC sense (see Chapter 1), stops existing on the server side: it is the client, whatever it may be, that decides how (or whether) to present the data received.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
text:
7.9 Stateful vs. Stateless
Chapter 5 presented a stateful model: the server keeps, in the HttpSession, information about each authenticated user, and every subsequent request is interpreted in light of that memory. A stateless service follows the opposite principle: the server keeps no memory at all between requests, and each request must carry, within itself, all the information needed to be processed — including, if required, proof that whoever is making it is authenticated.
This does not mean the application as a whole stops having persistent data — the database keeps storing countries, users, orders. It only means that the application server itself keeps no session information about who is making each request, from one request to the next.
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)
section: 7.10 Why the Absence of State Matters
text:
7.10 Why the Absence of State Matters
The limitation of the stateful model only becomes visible once there is more than one server instance answering requests — a common situation in any application with a real need to scale. If a user authenticates on instance A, and a following request is routed to instance B, that second instance has no corresponding session in its memory: the user appears unauthenticated, despite having just logged in.
A stateless service does not suffer from this problem: since no instance keeps memory of anyone, any one of them can answer any request, indifferently. This property is what makes it possible to distribute requests across several server instances with no coordination between them at all — a topic picked up in detail in Chapter 8.






POST + operation as an alternative to “pure” HTTP verbs



In practice, it is common to find APIs that do not follow the “pure” semantics of HTTP verbs presented above (POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove). A pragmatic alternative, used especially in contexts with technical constraints — for example, when only GET/POST requests can be issued, as from a simple HTML form, with no JavaScript involved (see Chapter 2) — is to concentrate write operations in a single endpoint, always received via POST, distinguishing the intended operation through an additional parameter, such as operation (insert, update, delete).
This solution works, but moves away from more conventional REST design: a single endpoint no longer maps directly to a resource and a verb, drifting instead towards an RPC style over HTTP. In an API designed to be consumed by JavaScript — which can issue PUT and DELETE requests with no limitation at all (see Chapter 8) — the closer-to-REST alternative is to rewrite that endpoint as several, one per HTTP verb (for example, PUT /resource/{id} to update and DELETE /resource/{id} to remove).
crumbs: 7  REST Web Services and Stateless Architecture (Part 1)

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.1 Session Limitations in Distributed Systems
Chapter 7 ended by pointing at the problem: an authentication model based on HttpSession (see Chapter 5) requires the server to keep, in memory, the state of each authenticated user. As soon as there is more than one server instance, that memory is no longer automatically shared between them.
There are known workarounds for this problem — sticky sessions (always routing the same client to the same instance) or replicating sessions across instances — but both come at a cost: the first limits how requests can be distributed, and the second requires extra infrastructure just to keep instances synchronised. Neither solves the problem at its root; both are ways of working around a dependency on state that, for a REST API (see Chapter 7), should not exist in the first place.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.2 Stateless Authentication: the Authorization Header
The stateless alternative reverses the responsibility: instead of the server keeping track of who is authenticated, it is the client itself that keeps proof of its authentication — a token — and resends it with every request, typically in the HTTP Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJqYXZhZWUifQ.dGhpc19pc19hX2Zha2Vfc2lnbmF0dXJl

The word Bearer indicates the type of credential that follows (literally, “bearer”: whoever presents this token is treated as its rightful owner). Upon receiving the request, the server does not need to consult any memory: it only needs to validate the token itself — what that is, and how that validation works, is the subject of the next section.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.3 JWT: a Stateless Token
A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a standardised token format, designed to carry information compactly and verifiably, without the server needing to keep anything about it. A JWT always has three parts, separated by dots:
<header>.<payload>.<signature>

Header

Metadata about the token itself, typically the signing algorithm used — for example, {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}

Payload

The data the token carries (the claims) — for example, {"sub":"javaee","role":"user","exp":1893456000}, identifying the user, their role, and the expiry date

Signature

The result of cryptographically signing the header and the payload with a secret key, known only to the server


Each of these three parts is encoded in Base64 and concatenated with dots, producing the long, unreadable string characteristic of a JWT (like the one in the Authorization header example above). The header and the payload are only encoded, not encrypted — anyone can read them, with no key needed. What guarantees that no one can forge a valid token is the signature: only whoever knows the server’s secret key can generate it correctly, and any change to the header or the payload, however small, invalidates the signature. Upon receiving a request, the server recomputes the signature from the received header and payload, and compares it with the one carried in the token: if they match, the content can be trusted, without the server having had to keep, itself, absolutely anything.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
text:
8.5 Horizontal Scalability
Scaling an application means increasing its capacity to answer more requests. There are, typically, two ways of doing this:

Vertical scalability

Increasing the resources (CPU, memory) of the existing machine — has a physical limit, and does not solve the problem of a single point of failure

Horizontal scalability

Adding more server instances, running in parallel, distributing requests between them — typically through a load balancer


Horizontal scalability only works without complications when any instance can answer any request, indifferently — exactly the property a stateless service offers. With JWT-based authentication, no instance needs to know anything about any other: each validates the received token completely independently, using the same secret key shared by all of them. It is this independence between instances that makes stateless architecture the foundation of any system designed to scale.
crumbs: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client

title: 8  REST Web Services (Part 2) and the JavaScript Client
section: 8.6 Distributed MVC: the Pattern Splits Across Server and Client
text:
8.6 Distributed MVC: the Pattern Splits Across Server and Client
In a presentation-oriented application, the MVC pattern (see Chapter 1) lives entirely on the server side: one component acts as Controller, and another, responsible for generating HTML, as View. In a REST API, that organisation stops making sense: the server no longer generates HTML, and the View, as defined in classic MVC, disappears from the server side.
On the server side, only the Model (data access) and the Controller (the endpoint that receives the HTTP request and returns JSON) remain. The role of View moves entirely to the client: it is the JavaScript code, running in the browser, that interprets the received JSON and manipulates the DOM to present it to whoever is using the application.
This split can be read as a second application of the same pattern, now on the client side: the JavaScript that handles the response and updates the page itself acts as both Controller (deciding what to do with the received response) and View (generating the HTML shown); the JSON returned by the API is the Model, kept on the server and synchronised on every fetch() request.
This is why a JavaScript front-office connected to a REST API is not an alternative to MVC, but rather the same pattern distributed across two machines instead of one.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.1 Introduction
Chapter 8 showed how a JWT (see Section 8.3) is signed and verified, without ever going into detail on which algorithm is used, or what security guarantees that signature actually offers. This appendix looks specifically at that question: token signing.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.2 HMAC: a Shared Secret Key
text:
B.2 HMAC: a Shared Secret Key
The algorithm used in Chapter 8, HS256, is the combination of HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) with the SHA-256 cryptographic hash function. It is a symmetric algorithm: the same secret key is used both to sign and to verify a token.
That key is never generated on the client, nor does it ever travel to it: it is created and stored exclusively on the server (typically once, during the application’s initial setup), and never leaves it. What the client receives, and later resends, is always the already-signed token — the result of using the key — never the key itself.






Figure B.1: In a symmetric scheme (HMAC), the same server holds the single secret key that exists, and uses it both to sign the token at login and to verify it on every subsequent request.



This works well in exactly the situation presented throughout this course: a single server (or several instances of that same server, all with access to the same secret key, see Section 8.5) is, at the same time, the one that issues tokens and the one that validates them. The key never leaves that trust boundary.
The drawback of HMAC appears when that boundary stops making sense: if an external system — one that should not have the authority to issue valid tokens — needed to validate them, it would have to receive the same secret key used to sign them. At that point, it stops being just a verifier: it also becomes capable of forging new, valid tokens, for any user.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.3 RSA and ECDSA: a Key Pair
text:
B.3 RSA and ECDSA: a Key Pair
An asymmetric algorithm solves this problem by splitting the two capabilities into two distinct keys: a private key, known only to whoever issues tokens, and a corresponding public key, which can be freely distributed to whoever needs to validate them. What the private key signs can only be verified with the corresponding public key — but it is not possible to sign anything new using only the public key.
The two most common asymmetric algorithms in JWT are RS256 (RSA with SHA-256) and ES256 (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with SHA-256) — the latter more recent, with smaller keys and faster verification for an equivalent security level, increasingly preferred over RSA in new systems.






Figure B.2: In an asymmetric scheme (RSA/ECDSA), only the Authentication Service holds the private key and signs new tokens; the corresponding public key can be freely distributed to any server that only needs to validate, without ever being able to issue tokens on another’s behalf.



This design is the usual one in systems made up of several independent services (sometimes called microservices): a single Authentication Service, responsible for validating credentials and issuing tokens, and several other services, each validating those tokens completely on its own, without ever communicating with each other, or trusting each other beyond the shared public key.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.4 Choosing Between HMAC and Asymmetric Signing
text:
B.4 Choosing Between HMAC and Asymmetric Signing









HMAC (HS256)
Asymmetric (RS256/ES256)




Number of keys
One, shared
Two: private (issues) and public (verifies)


Who can issue valid tokens
Anyone with the key
Only whoever has the private key


Who can validate tokens
Anyone with the key
Anyone with the public key


Typical scenario
One server (or trusted cluster) issues and validates
Several independent services only validate


Performance
Faster, simpler
Slower, larger keys (except ECDSA)



For the “World Capitals” application used throughout this course — a single server, responsible both for issuing and for validating its own tokens — HMAC is a perfectly adequate choice, which is why Chapter 8 uses it as its example. The choice would only start to favour an asymmetric algorithm if the application grew into several independent services, each of which should be able to validate, but not issue, access credentials.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.5 The alg:none Attack
The header of a JWT itself declares which algorithm was used for the signature (see Section 8.3). The original JWT specification allows, among the possible values for that field, the value none — intended for cases where integrity is already guaranteed by some other mechanism, and no signature is even needed.
A poorly implemented verifier, one that blindly trusts the algorithm declared in the header instead of enforcing an expected algorithm, can be fooled by a token like this one:
{"alg": "none", "typ": "JWT"}
followed by an arbitrary payload and an empty signature. If the verification code does not explicitly reject the none algorithm, an attacker can build, by hand, a token with any payload they want — for example, {"sub":"admin","role":"admin"} — without needing to know any key at all, and the server accepts it as legitimate.
It is exactly this attack that motivates the recommendation already made in Chapter 8: a well-written library, such as JJWT, requires the expected algorithm to be stated explicitly in the verification code, and rejects any token that declares a different algorithm — including none — regardless of what the token itself claims about itself.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
section: B.6 Where to Store the Token on the Client
text:
B.6 Where to Store the Token on the Client
Everything covered so far protects the token against forgery — but not against theft (see Section 8.2): whoever holds it can use it freely, as if they were its rightful owner, until it expires. Where the client stores it between requests determines what kind of theft it is exposed to.

Storing it in the browser’s localStorage

Accessible to any JavaScript code running on the page — including, unfortunately, a malicious script injected through a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability. If such a vulnerability exists in the application, an attacker can read the token directly and resend it, impersonating the user. On the other hand, it is not automatically sent by the browser in requests to other sites, so it is not exposed to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

HttpOnly cookie

Marked with the HttpOnly attribute, a cookie becomes inaccessible to the page’s own JavaScript — not even a malicious script can read it, which neutralises theft via XSS. In exchange, the browser automatically resends cookies on any request to the domain, even when that request is triggered by a page from another site — reopening the door to CSRF, which then has to be mitigated separately (for example, with the SameSite attribute)






localStorage
HttpOnly cookie




Accessible to JavaScript
Yes
No


Vulnerable to XSS theft
Yes
No


Automatically resent by the browser
No
Yes


Vulnerable to CSRF
No
Yes, requires separate mitigation



Neither option is risk-free — each trades one kind of vulnerability for another. The model followed in Chapter 8 (token resent manually in the Authorization header, see Section 8.7) assumes the token is accessible to the page’s own JavaScript, which points to localStorage, and is the most common approach in modern single-page applications. In that model, preventing XSS stops being just a general best practice: it becomes an essential condition for the security of the authentication mechanism itself — even though preventing XSS itself falls outside the scope of this appendix.

title: Appendix B — JWT Token Signing
text:
B.7 Minimum Best Practices

Never blindly accept the token’s declared algorithm — the verification code must explicitly enforce the expected algorithm (see Section B.5)
The secret (HMAC) or private (RSA/ECDSA) key must never live in the source code — it should be read from an environment variable or a dedicated secrets manager, never committed to a repository
A short or predictable key defeats the algorithm’s security — the recommended minimum length depends on the algorithm, but a short, memorable string is never appropriate
A short expiry (the exp claim, see Section 8.4) limits the damage from a compromised token, even with no additional mechanism
HTTPS is always mandatory — even a correctly signed token is a valid credential if it is intercepted in transit; the signature protects against forgery, not against network eavesdropping

These practices are a starting point, not an exhaustive treatment of Web application security.

title: Appendix C — Development Environment Setup
text:
C.1 Introduction
This appendix gathers, in a single place, all the tools needed throughout this course, with their installation links, official documentation, and possible alternatives.
The instructions and links below apply equally to macOS, Windows and Linux — every tool listed has a version for all three systems. Where a step depends on the operating system, this is explicitly flagged.

title: Appendix C — Development Environment Setup
section: C.2 The Tools for This Course
text:
C.2 The Tools for This Course

JDK — Java Development Kit

The Java language and the tools to compile and run it — the foundation for everything else. The Eclipse Temurin distribution is recommended: free, open source, maintained by the Eclipse Adoptium Working Group, and available for all three operating systems. Alternative: Oracle JDK, Oracle’s official build, under a different licence. Help: official documentation at https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/; for specific questions, the java tag on Stack Overflow is the first place to check.

Apache Tomcat

The Servlet Container used throughout the course (see Chapter 4), installed on the server side. Available at https://tomcat.apache.org/. Alternatives exist (Jetty, or a full application server such as WildFly, already mentioned in Chapter 4), but they are not used in this course. Help: official documentation at https://tomcat.apache.org/tomcat-10.1-doc/; the tomcat tag on Stack Overflow for specific questions.

Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers

The development environment (IDE) used for server-side code (Servlets, Filters, JSP), with built-in support for Jakarta EE projects and for installing and managing Tomcat directly from within Eclipse. Downloaded from https://www.eclipse.org/downloads/packages/ (choose exactly the “Enterprise Java and Web Developers” package, not the generic “Eclipse IDE for Java Developers” package, which does not include the Web project tools). Alternative: IntelliJ IDEA (the Ultimate edition, paid — but free for students on registration — includes equivalent Jakarta EE support; the free Community edition does not). Help: Eclipse community forum; the eclipse tag on Stack Overflow.

VSCode or WebStorm

A lighter editor, used for client-side code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, see Chapter 2 and Chapter 8) — it does not need either of Eclipse’s two Java EE-specific supports. VSCode is free and cross-platform; WebStorm is paid (free for students on registration), more specialised in JavaScript. Help: official documentation at https://code.visualstudio.com/docs (VSCode) or https://www.jetbrains.com/webstorm/documentation/ (WebStorm).

A modern browser, with developer tools

Chrome, Firefox and Edge all work equally well; what matters is knowing how to open their developer tools (DevTools, F12 key or Cmd+Option+I on Mac), used throughout the course to inspect network requests and debug JavaScript (see Chapter 8). Help: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/ (Chrome) or https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/devtools-user/ (Firefox).

A REST client

A tool for building HTTP requests by hand (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, with headers and body of your choosing), useful for testing a REST API directly (see Chapter 7) without depending on any front-office already built. A simple GET can always be tested directly in the browser, but POST, PUT and DELETE cannot. Postman is the best known; Insomnia is a lighter alternative; whoever prefers the command line can use curl, already included by default on macOS, on Linux, and on Windows 10 and later.

MySQL or MariaDB

The relational database management system used from LAB4 onward (Appendix G), when the fixed data used in the earlier LABs is replaced with real data, accessed through JDBC. MySQL Community Server is the free, open-source edition of MySQL; MariaDB Server is a free, open-source alternative, directly compatible (same network protocol, same JDBC driver) — either one works for this course. To create and manage the tables without relying solely on the command line, it is also useful to install a graphical client, such as MySQL Workbench or DBeaver (cross-platform, compatible with both MySQL and MariaDB). Help: official documentation at https://dev.mysql.com/doc/ (MySQL) or https://mariadb.com/kb/en/documentation/ (MariaDB); the mysql and mariadb tags on Stack Overflow for specific questions.

LABs 1 to 5 build the entire backend: each one is tested directly in the browser or with a REST client (see Appendix C), with no JavaScript at all. title: Appendix D — LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
section: D.2 LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
text:
D.2 LAB1: First Endpoint and Simulated DAO
A good development environment setup is the foundation of any robust, maintainable application. Investing time up front in correctly preparing the tools and structuring the project saves, later on, countless hours of debugging and reorganising. This LAB guides the configuration of Eclipse and Tomcat, and the creation of the first endpoint, which will serve as the API’s “health check”.

D.2.1 Step 1.1: Prepare the Development Environment

Install the Eclipse IDE: start by downloading and installing “Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers” (see Appendix C). It is important to choose exactly this edition, since it comes pre-configured with the essential tools for this project
Install Apache Tomcat (see Appendix C for the required version), following the installation instructions, outside Eclipse
Configure Apache Tomcat in Eclipse:

In Eclipse, go to the Servers perspective. If it is not visible, open it via Window > Show View > Servers
Click the link to create a new server (“No servers are available. Click this link to create a new server…”)
In the window that appears, expand the Apache folder and select the installed Tomcat version
Follow the wizard’s steps, pointing to the folder where Tomcat was installed
Once finished, the Tomcat server appears in the Servers perspective, ready to use




D.2.2 Step 1.2: Create the Dynamic Web Project

From the Eclipse menu, select File > New > Dynamic Web Project
In the project creation window, set the Project name to CapitaisAPI
Confirm that the Target runtime is set to the Apache Tomcat server configured in the previous step
Click Finish to create the project
Once the project is created, it is good practice to organise the source code into packages: in the Project Explorer, expand the “Java Resources” section and locate the source folder (usually src or src/main/java). Right-click that folder, New > Package, and create the package capitaisapi.servlets



D.2.3 Step 1.3: Develop the First Endpoint (Servlet)
The first endpoint is a simple status checker, to confirm that the API is working correctly.

Right-click the capitaisapi.servlets package just created, New > Servlet
In the window that opens, keep all fields at their pre-filled value, and name the class StatusServlet. Click Finish
Eclipse generates the class skeleton. Map this Servlet to the /status URL through the @WebServlet annotation, directly above the class declaration (it becomes @WebServlet("/status"))
Test the Servlet: in the file explorer, right-click the file containing the Servlet, Run As > Run on Server. Choose the Tomcat server of the same version used when creating the Servlet, and Finish. Within a few seconds, the Servlet’s result should appear in a browser
Create a new Servlet, following the same process, in the same package, called CountryCapital, and change the doGet method to return a simple JSON message. This method is invoked whenever an HTTP GET request is made to the /countrycapital URL. To write this method according to HTTP requirements and good programming practice (see Chapter 4), replace all of doGet()’s code with this:

// Inside the doGet method of the CountryCapital Servlet
response.setContentType("application/json"); // sets the content type to JSON
PrintWriter out = response.getWriter(); // obtains the output stream

// Manual construction of the JSON String
String jsonResponse = "{\"country\": \"Portugal\", \"capital\": \"Lisboa\", \"ccode\": \"PT\"}";
out.print(jsonResponse); // sends the structured data to the client
out.flush();
PrintWriter needs to be imported, since it is not included in the Servlet’s generated skeleton. Note that the JSON String contains quotes inside it — so the quotes inside the Java String have to be written as \" (escaped). Do not use single quotes inside the String, since they are not valid in JSON.


D.2.4 Step 1.4: Deploy and Test the Application

Test the Servlet again, exactly as in Step 1.3 (point 4). Eclipse compiles, deploys and starts the application on the server
It is also possible to test by right-clicking the project name (CapitaisAPI) — this opens a browser (or a testing tool). Enter the following URL:
http://localhost:8080/CapitaisAPI/countrycapital
The following response should appear on screen:
{"country": "Portugal", "capital": "Lisboa", "ccode": "PT"}

confirming that the first endpoint is working correctly. While the Servlet is running on the server, the browser can be closed and reopened, entering the same URL, and the result stays the same.


D.2.5 Step 1.5: Implement the Database Interface via a DAO
In a “real-life” application, dynamic content is normally generated from data coming from a database. The link between the Web application and the database can be made through a Data Access Object (DAO, see Chapter 4), which hides the database’s implementation details from the Web application. This application will use a DAO to interface between the Web application and the database.
Since there is no access to a real database yet, this stage of the project will use a DAO that simulates access to the database (later, in LAB4, this DAO will be changed to query a real database). Note that, from the Web application’s point of view, there is no difference at all between a DAO that fetches data from a real database and one that has the data fixed directly in the code.
Create a new class, called DBDAO, in the capitaisapi.dao package, and write three public methods in it:

List<String> getCountryCodes();
String getCountryName(String countryCode);
String getCapitalName(String countryCode);

The first method returns the list of available country codes (PT, FR, EN, etc.), the second returns the country name associated with a code, and the last returns the capital name associated with a country code.
For this LAB, fix all return values directly in the DBDAO class’s code. Use a HashMap<String, String> to hold the fixed values of country codes and capital names, and a List to hold the list of country codes.
By default, the /countrycapital Servlet should show the capital of the first country in the list returned by the DAO’s List<String> getCountryCodes() method.


D.2.6 Step 1.6: Create the Data Model (POJO)
To represent the application’s data in a structured way, POJOs (Plain Old Java Objects) are used. A POJO is a data type, just like String or Integer, and so it helps guarantee that a given piece of information always follows the same rules. If a POJO is used as a method’s return value, that value comes to respect what is defined in the POJO — in other words, a POJO is a data model. It is created already at this stage, so that the main pieces are defined, even though the POJO will only actually be used further on.

Create a new class called CountryModel in the capitaisapi.servlets package. This will be the POJO
Add private attributes to represent a country’s data: codigo, nome and capital. Later, if convenient, others can be added, such as population or area
Generate the getters and setters for all attributes: right-click a blank line below the attribute definitions, Source > Generate Getters and Setters — Eclipse generates the code automatically



D.2.7 Step 1.7: Develop the Capitals Endpoint
A new Servlet is now created that uses the DAO to return dynamic data. For testing purposes, the DAO should not return all of a country’s information (code, name and capital) — the POJO is only used when it is necessary to return a country’s complete information.

Create a new Servlet called CapitalServlet, in the capitaisapi.servlets package, mapped to the /capital URL
In the doGet method, implement the logic to:

Read the countrycode parameter from the request (request.getParameter("countrycode"))
Instantiate DBDAO and call getCapitalName() with the received country code
Check whether the country was found: if so, build a JSON String with the country code and the capital name; if not, return an appropriate error response. If the countrycode parameter is null or empty, return 400 (missing parameter, see Chapter 3); if countrycode has an unknown value, return 404 (country not found). Use response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST) for 400, and response.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_NOT_FOUND) for 404
Set the Content-Type to application/json, and send the JSON String as the response




D.2.8 Step 1.8: Develop the Countries Endpoint

Create a new Servlet CountryServlet, in the same package as the previous ones, mapped to /country
In DBDAO, add a new method CountryModel getCountry(String countrycode), meant to return all of a country’s data (code, country name and capital name)
Using a structure similar to CapitalServlet’s, in the doGet method, obtain a country’s complete data and return the complete JSON structure, properly validated by the CountryModel POJO

Note that the Servlet no longer manipulates isolated data (loose Strings), and instead works with a structured object — which improves readability, maintainability and data validation. The getCountry() method in DBDAO now centralises the aggregation of the data and encapsulates it in a structured model (POJO), reducing the Servlet’s responsibility.

E.1 LAB2: Login and Session
Security is a fundamental concern in any Web application. Since this is a REST API, redirects are not used as in a traditional Web application — all communication with the client happens through HTTP status codes and JSON bodies (see Chapter 3). In this LAB, a login endpoint is added to the “World Capitals API”, and the HTTP session (see Chapter 5) is used to keep track, on the server side, of the fact that a given user is authenticated.

title: Appendix H — LAB5 (Optional): Stateless Authentication with JWT
text:
H.1 LAB5 (Optional): Stateless Authentication with JWT
In LABs 1 to 4, server-side stateful authentication was implemented (HttpSession). This model is common in traditional Java Web applications, and is a good way of clearly understanding authentication and authorization.
In this optional LAB, the project evolves towards a modern, stateless REST API architecture: HttpSession and JSESSIONID are no longer used, the server stops keeping any per-user state between requests, and authentication is instead done with a JWT (JSON Web Token, see Chapter 8 and Appendix B), sent with every protected request. This LAB is optional, aimed at anyone who wants to go further and understand how modern APIs typically authenticate clients.
Objectives: by the end of this LAB, it should be possible to explain the difference between stateful (session) authentication and stateless (token) authentication; implement JWT-based authentication; use the HTTP Authorization header with the Bearer scheme; validate a JWT inside a Filter; and correctly distinguish 401 from 403.
